title: Inspector Sharma: The Missing Manuscript
description: A priceless manuscript of Kalidasa's original Abhijnanasakuntalam has vanished from the National Museum in New Delhi. You are Inspector Sharma of the Delhi Police Crime Branch, called in to solve the case before the manuscript is smuggled out of India. Interview witnesses, examine clues, navigate the politics of art theft, and piece together the mystery. But be careful -- every investigation has consequences, and your reputation is on the line. Will you find the manuscript and the culprit, or will this cold case define your career?
learning_objectives: Develop logical reasoning and deductive thinking through detective investigation
Learn about India's cultural heritage, museum systems, and art preservation
Understand the Indian legal system, evidence handling, and investigation procedures
Build critical thinking skills by evaluating witness statements and evidence
Explore ethical dilemmas in law enforcement and the importance of due process

how_to_play.title: How to Play
steps: You are Inspector Sharma investigating the theft of a priceless manuscript from the National Museum, Delhi
Each round presents a new lead, witness, or piece of evidence to examine
Choose how to proceed -- interview techniques, forensic analysis, or field investigation
Monitor your Evidence, Suspicion Level, Time Remaining, and Reputation as you investigate
Too much suspicion on the wrong person can lead to wrongful accusations
Solve the case before time runs out while maintaining your professional reputation
tips: Gather evidence before accusing anyone -- wrongful accusations destroy your reputation
Time is limited; prioritize leads that yield the most evidence
High suspicion on the wrong person can mislead your investigation
Pay attention to inconsistencies in witness statements
Sometimes the most obvious suspect is not the real culprit

rounds.title: Round 1: The Crime Scene
rounds.story: You arrive at the National Museum on Janpath, New Delhi. The manuscript display case is shattered, but the museum's CCTV footage from last night is mysteriously corrupted. The night security guard, Ramesh, is visibly nervous. The museum curator, Dr. Meenakshi Iyer, is frantic. You notice three things: scratch marks on the display case lock, a faint perfume smell near the case, and muddy footprints leading toward the emergency exit. You have limited time -- which lead do you pursue first?
rounds.goal: Choose your first investigative action at the crime scene wisely to establish strong initial leads.

choices.label: Dust for Fingerprints on the Case
choices.feedback: Your forensic team lifts three sets of fingerprints from the case. In India, the Fingerprint Bureau in Kolkata, established in 1897, was the world's first such bureau. Sir Edward Henry developed the fingerprint classification system while serving in Bengal. Forensic evidence is the backbone of modern investigation -- it does not lie, unlike witnesses.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: Your forensic team lifts three sets of fingerprints from the case. In India, the Fingerprint Bureau in Kolkata, established in 1897, was the world's first such bureau.

choices.label: Interrogate the Nervous Security Guard
choices.feedback: Ramesh admits he fell asleep for 30 minutes during his shift. He is terrified of losing his job. Under Indian law (CrPC Section 161), witnesses must answer police questions truthfully. Ramesh's nervousness may be guilt or simply fear. Be careful not to jump to conclusions -- in many wrongful convictions, investigators focused too early on the easiest suspect.

choices.label: Follow the Muddy Footprints
choices.feedback: The footprints lead to the museum's back garden, then to a gap in the boundary wall near Rajpath. The mud is distinctive red laterite soil -- common in parts of South Delhi near Mehrauli. This narrows down where the thief may have come from. Systematic evidence collection, like following physical trails, is what separates good detective work from guesswork.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: The footprints lead to the museum's back garden, then to a gap in the boundary wall near Rajpath. The mud is distinctive red laterite soil -- common in parts of South Delhi near Mehrauli.

rounds.coaching_moment: Consider how this choice affects your long-term resources, not just the immediate gain.
rounds.reflection_prompt: What tradeoff did this decision reveal? What did you gain, and what did you give up?

rounds.title: Round 2: The Curator's Secret
rounds.story: Dr. Meenakshi Iyer, the museum curator, provides you with a list of people who had access to the manuscript room's keycard. There are five names. However, when you check the museum's digital access logs, you discover that Dr. Iyer herself accessed the manuscript room at 11:47 PM -- just 13 minutes before the estimated theft time. When confronted, she turns pale and says, 'I was doing a routine check. I do that sometimes.' Her hands are trembling. The museum director calls, pressuring you to solve this quietly to avoid a media scandal.
rounds.goal: Decide how to handle the curator's suspicious behaviour while managing pressure from the museum administration.

choices.label: Press Dr. Iyer Harder in Interrogation
choices.feedback: Under pressure, Dr. Iyer reveals she was actually meeting someone secretly -- an international art dealer named Marcus Webb who wanted to photograph the manuscript. She was embarrassed about the unauthorized meeting. In Indian law, Section 176 of CrPC allows magistrates to inquire into suspicious circumstances. Sometimes people hide things not because they are guilty, but because they fear judgment.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: Under pressure, Dr. Iyer reveals she was actually meeting someone secretly -- an international art dealer named Marcus Webb who wanted to photograph the manuscript.

choices.label: Quietly Investigate the Access Logs Further
choices.feedback: You discover that another keycard -- belonging to a recently resigned employee named Vikram Thakur -- was also used at 12:02 AM, after the theft window. This is crucial evidence! The Digital Personal Data Protection Act of India emphasizes the importance of digital records. Your methodical approach preserves trust and uncovers a stronger lead than pressuring the curator would have.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: You discover that another keycard -- belonging to a recently resigned employee named Vikram Thakur -- was also used at 12:02 AM, after the theft window. This is crucial evidence! The Digital Personal Data Protection Act of India emphasizes the importance of digital records.

choices.label: Report Everything Transparently to Media
choices.feedback: You hold a brief press conference. The media attention generates tips from the public. India's Right to Information Act (2005) established transparency as a democratic principle. While the museum director is upset, the public's right to know about heritage crime is important. Transparency in investigation builds public trust, though it can also alert the thief.

rounds.title: Round 3: The Art Dealer's Trail
rounds.story: Your investigation leads to Marcus Webb, a British art dealer staying at The Imperial Hotel on Janpath. His room contains catalogues of ancient Indian manuscripts with market prices -- the Kalidasa manuscript is valued at 50 crore rupees internationally. Webb claims he is a legitimate dealer, but his phone records show calls to an underground antiquities network operating between Delhi and Dubai. You also find that Webb has a flight booked to Dubai in 36 hours. The Archaeological Survey of India (ASI) confirms the manuscript is protected under the Antiquities and Art Treasures Act, 1972.
rounds.goal: Decide how to handle the international art dealer while working within Indian law to prevent the manuscript from leaving the country.

choices.label: Arrest Webb Immediately
choices.feedback: You arrest Webb, but his lawyer arrives within the hour citing lack of direct evidence linking him to the theft. Under the Antiquities and Art Treasures Act (1972), possessing catalogues is not illegal. The arrest may not hold up in court. In India, Article 22 of the Constitution guarantees the right to legal counsel. Premature arrests can weaken your case and damage your reputation with the judiciary.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: You arrest Webb, but his lawyer arrives within the hour citing lack of direct evidence linking him to the theft. Under the Antiquities and Art Treasures Act (1972), possessing catalogues is not illegal.

choices.label: Place Webb Under Surveillance
choices.feedback: You deploy a surveillance team. Over 24 hours, Webb meets with two local contacts in Paharganj -- a known hub for antique smuggling. One contact matches the description of Vikram Thakur, the resigned museum employee! Surveillance requires patience but yields strong evidence. The Intelligence Bureau of India uses similar methods for tracking art smuggling networks that operate across borders.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: You deploy a surveillance team. Over 24 hours, Webb meets with two local contacts in Paharganj -- a known hub for antique smuggling.

choices.label: Alert Interpol and Immigration
choices.feedback: You contact the CBI's Interpol division and flag Webb's passport. If the manuscript crosses borders, it becomes an international crime. India has been working with Interpol and UNESCO to recover stolen antiquities -- in recent years, hundreds of stolen idols and artefacts have been returned to India. International cooperation is essential when cultural heritage crime crosses borders.

rounds.title: Round 4: The Underground Market
rounds.story: Your surveillance team tracks Vikram Thakur to a shop in the lanes of Chandni Chowk in Old Delhi. The shop, 'Heritage Collectibles,' appears to sell tourist souvenirs but has a hidden back room. Your informant tells you this shop is part of a network that smuggles antiquities through Nepal and Dubai. Entering without a warrant could compromise the case, but waiting for a warrant might give them time to move the manuscript. A local Sub-Inspector offers to 'handle it informally' -- suggesting he knows someone who can get you inside without paperwork.
rounds.goal: Navigate the tension between urgency and legal procedure in the investigation.

choices.label: Get a Proper Search Warrant from the Magistrate
choices.feedback: You approach the Metropolitan Magistrate under Section 93 of CrPC for a search warrant. It takes 10 hours, but the warrant is airtight. When you raid the shop, everything found is admissible in court. The Indian Constitution's Article 20(3) protects against self-incrimination, and Article 21 ensures due process. Legal shortcuts may seem efficient but destroy cases in court.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: You approach the Metropolitan Magistrate under Section 93 of CrPC for a search warrant. It takes 10 hours, but the warrant is airtight.

choices.label: Accept the Sub-Inspector's Informal Help
choices.feedback: The Sub-Inspector gets you inside, but the methods are questionable. Any evidence found may be challenged in court under the Indian Evidence Act as 'fruit of the poisonous tree.' India's Supreme Court has repeatedly held that illegally obtained evidence can be excluded. Shortcuts in policing erode public trust and the rule of law -- a lesson many officers learn too late.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: The Sub-Inspector gets you inside, but the methods are questionable. Any evidence found may be challenged in court under the Indian Evidence Act as 'fruit of the poisonous tree.

choices.label: Send an Undercover Officer as a Buyer
choices.feedback: Your undercover officer poses as a wealthy NRI collector. The shop owner shows him a catalogue that includes a Kalidasa manuscript listed as 'available soon.' This is strong circumstantial evidence! Undercover operations are a legitimate law enforcement technique recognized under Indian law, though they require careful documentation to hold up in court.

rounds.title: Round 5: The Whistleblower
rounds.story: A young museum intern named Priya Nair contacts you anonymously. She says she has information about the theft but fears for her safety. She works part-time at the museum to fund her History degree from JNU. Priya claims she saw Vikram Thakur and another senior museum official, Assistant Director Rajesh Kapoor, behaving suspiciously near the manuscript room on multiple occasions before the theft. She wants protection before she will testify. The Whistleblowers Protection Act exists, but implementation is inconsistent.
rounds.goal: Decide how to handle the whistleblower's information while ensuring her safety and maintaining investigation integrity.

choices.label: Formally Register Her as a Protected Witness
choices.feedback: You invoke the Witness Protection Scheme (2018) approved by the Supreme Court of India. Priya is given identity protection and a safe location. She provides detailed testimony about Vikram and Kapoor's meetings. India's witness protection framework is still evolving -- the Supreme Court recognized it as a fundamental right under Article 21. Protecting whistleblowers strengthens the justice system.

choices.label: Meet Her Secretly and Keep It Off Record
choices.feedback: You meet Priya at a cafe near India Gate. She shares crucial details but refuses to go on record. Off-record information can guide your investigation but cannot be used as evidence in court. Under the Indian Evidence Act, hearsay evidence is generally inadmissible. While this saves time, it creates a legal vulnerability if the case goes to trial.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: You meet Priya at a cafe near India Gate. She shares crucial details but refuses to go on record.

choices.label: Confront Assistant Director Kapoor Directly
choices.feedback: Kapoor vehemently denies involvement and immediately calls the Culture Ministry. His political connections create pressure on your department. Confronting a suspect without sufficient evidence can backfire badly. In the Indian bureaucratic system, senior officials often have powerful networks. This is why building a strong evidence base before confrontation is crucial -- as the saying goes, 'shoot only when you are sure of your aim.'
choices.counterfactual_feedback: Kapoor vehemently denies involvement and immediately calls the Culture Ministry. His political connections create pressure on your department.

rounds.title: Round 6: The Digital Trail
rounds.story: Your cyber cell discovers that Vikram Thakur used a VPN to communicate with an encrypted messaging app. However, they manage to recover metadata showing that Thakur received payments totalling 15 lakh rupees from an offshore account in the Cayman Islands, routed through a hawala network. The financial trail connects to Marcus Webb's company. Your tech team can attempt to crack the full encryption, but it requires a court order under the Information Technology Act. Meanwhile, a journalist from NDTV has caught wind of the investigation and is about to publish a story.
rounds.goal: Balance digital investigation with legal requirements and media management in a high-profile case.

choices.label: Get Court Order for Digital Evidence Under IT Act
choices.feedback: You obtain an order under Section 69 of the Information Technology Act (2000) for lawful interception. The decrypted messages reveal the entire plan -- Thakur was recruited by Kapoor, who connected with Webb's smuggling network. Digital evidence obtained through proper legal channels is admissible and powerful. India's IT Act provides a framework for cybercrime investigation while protecting privacy rights.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: You obtain an order under Section 69 of the Information Technology Act (2000) for lawful interception. The decrypted messages reveal the entire plan -- Thakur was recruited by Kapoor, who connected with Webb's smuggling network.

choices.label: Trace the Hawala Network Through ED
choices.feedback: You coordinate with the Enforcement Directorate (ED), which investigates financial crimes under FEMA and PMLA. The hawala trail reveals that this is not the first theft -- the network has been smuggling Indian antiquities for years. Hawala, meaning 'transfer' in Arabic, is an informal money transfer system. While it has legitimate uses, it is often exploited for money laundering. The ED's involvement strengthens the financial crime angle of your case.

choices.label: Brief the Journalist Strategically
choices.feedback: You give the journalist a controlled briefing, revealing enough to generate public interest without compromising the investigation. The media coverage generates new tips from art dealers and collectors. India's press freedom, while not explicitly in the Constitution, is derived from Article 19(1)(a) -- freedom of speech and expression. Strategic media engagement can be a powerful investigative tool when handled carefully.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: You give the journalist a controlled briefing, revealing enough to generate public interest without compromising the investigation. The media coverage generates new tips from art dealers and collectors.

rounds.title: Round 7: The Net Closes
rounds.story: Your investigation has identified the full conspiracy: Assistant Director Kapoor recruited Vikram Thakur to steal the manuscript, Marcus Webb arranged international buyers, and the Chandni Chowk shop was the handover point. But there is a complication -- the manuscript has already been moved from the shop. Your surveillance team spots Thakur heading to Indira Gandhi International Airport with a large, flat package. Webb is at The Imperial Hotel packing his bags. Kapoor is in his office at the museum, acting normal. You have enough officers for two simultaneous operations.
rounds.goal: Choose your tactical priorities for the arrest operation, knowing you can only be in two places at once.

choices.label: Rush to Airport + Arrest Webb at Hotel
choices.feedback: You intercept Thakur at IGI Airport Terminal 3 just before security check. The package contains the manuscript, carefully wrapped in acid-free paper. Webb is arrested at The Imperial with incriminating documents. Under CISF jurisdiction at airports, your coordination with airport security is seamless. The manuscript is recovered! India's airport security protocols, managed by CISF and Bureau of Immigration, are designed to prevent exactly this kind of smuggling.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: You intercept Thakur at IGI Airport Terminal 3 just before security check. The package contains the manuscript, carefully wrapped in acid-free paper.

choices.label: Coordinate All Three Arrests Simultaneously
choices.feedback: You coordinate with local police for three simultaneous operations. The synchronization is challenging but prevents any suspect from alerting the others. This mirrors how the CBI conducts raids in major cases -- simultaneous action across multiple locations. All three are caught, but Thakur nearly escapes in the airport confusion. Coordination between agencies (Delhi Police, CISF, and Crime Branch) is what makes or breaks complex operations.

choices.label: Arrest Kapoor First (He May Destroy Evidence)
choices.feedback: You arrest Kapoor at the museum, seizing his computer and phone before he can delete anything. His devices contain the entire communication history with Webb. However, the delay means Thakur almost makes it onto his flight -- your team barely stops him at the boarding gate. Securing digital evidence from the mastermind is smart, but the manuscript's safety should always be the top priority in heritage crime.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: You arrest Kapoor at the museum, seizing his computer and phone before he can delete anything. His devices contain the entire communication history with Webb.

rounds.title: Round 8: Justice and Legacy
rounds.story: The manuscript is recovered and all three suspects are in custody. The case has become national news. The Culture Ministry wants a quick resolution, the museum wants to minimize scandal, and the court requires a watertight chargesheet. You must now prepare the final case presentation. The CJM (Chief Judicial Magistrate) will review your chargesheet under Section 173 of CrPC. How you present the case will determine whether justice is served and whether India's cultural heritage protection improves as a result.
rounds.goal: Choose how to present the case to ensure maximum justice, systemic reform, and protection of India's cultural heritage.

choices.label: File Comprehensive Chargesheet with All Evidence
choices.feedback: Your chargesheet is 200 pages of meticulously documented evidence -- fingerprints, digital trails, financial records, witness testimony, and forensic analysis. Under Section 173 of CrPC, a well-prepared chargesheet is crucial for conviction. The court appreciates your thoroughness. This case becomes a landmark reference for future heritage crime prosecutions in India, strengthening the Antiquities and Art Treasures Act enforcement.

choices.label: File Chargesheet + Recommend Museum Security Reforms
choices.feedback: Beyond the criminal case, you submit recommendations for museum security upgrades, mandatory CCTV backup systems, and stricter access controls. The ASI and National Museum adopt several recommendations. In India, institutions like the National Museum, ASI, and INTACH work to protect our 5,000+ year heritage. Your investigation does not just catch criminals -- it helps prevent future thefts. Systemic reform is the highest form of justice.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: Beyond the criminal case, you submit recommendations for museum security upgrades, mandatory CCTV backup systems, and stricter access controls. The ASI and National Museum adopt several recommendations.

choices.label: Negotiate Plea Deal for Thakur's Full Testimony
choices.feedback: Thakur agrees to testify against Kapoor and Webb in exchange for a reduced sentence. His testimony exposes the full international network. Plea bargaining was introduced in Indian criminal law through Chapter XXIA of CrPC (2006 amendment). While controversial, it can be effective for dismantling larger criminal networks. The international smuggling ring is exposed, leading to recoveries of other stolen artefacts across multiple countries.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: Thakur agrees to testify against Kapoor and Webb in exchange for a reduced sentence. His testimony exposes the full international network.

glossary_terms.definition: A formal document filed by police under Section 173 of CrPC after completing investigation. It contains the evidence, list of witnesses, and charges against the accused. Filing a chargesheet within the stipulated time is crucial -- otherwise the accused may get default bail.
glossary_terms.deep_dive: A chargesheet (or charge sheet) is a formal document filed by police in court listing criminal charges against an accused. In India, it must be filed within 60-90 days of arrest under CrPC Section 173. It includes evidence, witness statements, and the specific sections of law violated. Courts can reject chargesheets lacking sufficient evidence — making its preparation a critical legal step.
glossary_terms.real_world_example: When investigating corporate fraud, a chargesheet might list charges of cheating (IPC 420), forgery (IPC 465), and criminal breach of trust (IPC 406) — each charge requiring specific evidence. A weak chargesheet with circumstantial-only evidence often leads to bail being granted.

glossary_terms.definition: An Indian law that regulates the export, trade, and possession of antiquities. Any object over 100 years old is classified as an antiquity. The Act makes it illegal to export antiquities without a license from the ASI and aims to prevent the looting of India's cultural heritage.
glossary_terms.deep_dive: This Act regulates the export and trade of antiquities (objects over 100 years old) and art treasures in India. It requires registration of antiques with the Archaeological Survey of India (ASI). Violation can lead to 6 months to 3 years imprisonment plus fine. The Act tries to prevent India's cultural heritage from being smuggled abroad — a major problem given India's rich archaeological history.
glossary_terms.real_world_example: In 2021, Interpol's Operation Thunder recovered 82 cultural objects illegally exported from India. Without the 1972 Act's registration system, proving ownership and demanding repatriation of these objects from foreign museums and private collectors would have been nearly impossible.

glossary_terms.definition: An informal money transfer system where money is paid to an agent in one location and an equivalent amount is disbursed by another agent in a different location. While not inherently illegal, it is regulated under FEMA and often used for illicit transfers.
glossary_terms.deep_dive: Hawala is an informal value transfer system based on trust and a network of brokers (hawaladars). Money is NOT physically moved — a broker in Mumbai takes cash and calls a counterpart in Dubai, who delivers equivalent funds locally. Records are often minimal. While illegal in India under FEMA, hawala is used for both legitimate remittances (faster/cheaper than banks) and money laundering.
glossary_terms.real_world_example: A terror financing investigation traced Rs 2 crore from Dubai to India via hawala — money that funded multiple attacks. Each hawala transaction left no direct bank trail, requiring investigators to build cases through informants, phone intercepts, and following the hawaladars' physical movements.

glossary_terms.definition: The main legislation governing the procedure for administration of criminal law in India. Enacted in 1973, it provides the machinery for investigation of crime, apprehension of suspects, collection of evidence, determination of guilt, and imposition of punishment.
glossary_terms.deep_dive: CrPC (now replaced by BNSS - Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita 2023) governed criminal procedure in India — from FIR filing to trial to sentencing. Key provisions: Section 41 (arrest without warrant), Section 161 (police questioning), Section 164 (magistrate statement), Section 173 (final report/chargesheet). Understanding CrPC is essential for any investigator to ensure evidence gathered is legally admissible.
glossary_terms.real_world_example: Police who interrogate a suspect without following CrPC Section 41A (notice of appearance) risk having confessions thrown out in court. In the 2G spectrum case, procedural lapses in evidence collection led to several acquittals despite strong documentary evidence of corruption.

glossary_terms.definition: A landmark Indian law that empowers citizens to request information from public authorities. It promotes transparency and accountability in government functioning. Any Indian citizen can file an RTI application to seek information from government bodies.
glossary_terms.deep_dive: RTI Act empowers citizens to request any information from government bodies within 30 days. Public Information Officers (PIOs) must respond or give reasons for denial. Exemptions include national security, third-party privacy, and cabinet deliberations. RTI has exposed thousands of corruption cases — from PDS grain diversion to fake degrees of politicians — making it one of India's most powerful accountability tools.
glossary_terms.real_world_example: An RTI application revealed that a Mumbai municipal corporation awarded 23 road contracts to 4 firms with the same registered address — evidence of cartelization that led to a CBI investigation. This single RTI filing by an activist uncovered ₹340 crore of suspected fraud.

replay_variants.label: The Curator Did It
replay_variants.summary: What if the suspicious-looking person was suspicious for a reason?
replay_variants.killer_motive: Mid-career curator passed over for the director role; sold the manuscript to fund a private collection she'd promised her late father

r2.twist: Dr. Iyer's trembling isn't shame — it's fear. The 11:47 PM access wasn't a routine check; it was the theft.

r3.twist: Marcus Webb is real but he's a buyer, not the thief. The trail leads back to the same museum office.

r5.twist: The auction house broker confirms the seller used a private collector pseudonym matching Iyer's father's name.

r7.twist: The forensic match on the manuscript fragment ties to a curator's tools, not a dealer's transport case.

replay_variants.label: The Insider Conspiracy
replay_variants.summary: What if it wasn't one person — it was three?
replay_variants.killer_name: The Security Chief, the Cataloguer, and a Trustee
replay_variants.killer_motive: A coordinated insider job: security chief disabled the camera, cataloguer altered the manifest, board trustee facilitated the buyer — all owed money after a botched 2022 deal

r1.twist: The crime scene is too clean — the gloves, the angle, the timing. Three people, not one, were here.

r4.twist: The CCTV gap isn't a malfunction. The security chief logged out remotely from his home laptop at 11:43 PM.

r6.twist: The forged manifest was edited from inside the museum LAN at 12:08 AM — the cataloguer's workstation.

r8.twist: The buyer's wire instructions trace to a holding company controlled by a current trustee.

replay_variants.label: The Outside Job
replay_variants.summary: What if Marcus Webb was the smokescreen and the real thief never set foot in India?
replay_variants.killer_name: An anonymous European collector working through a courier
replay_variants.killer_motive: A reclusive collector commissioned the theft 18 months in advance; Marcus Webb was the body double the collector deliberately let you find

r2.twist: Dr. Iyer's panic is unrelated — she was meeting a journalist, not a dealer.

r3.twist: Marcus Webb's trail is too perfect. Every clue points to him in a way no real thief would allow.

r5.twist: The auction house doesn't know the buyer's identity — only a coded reference and a Geneva wire account.

r7.twist: Forensics finds a courier's tape signature on the case — the manuscript left India within 6 hours of the theft.

replay_config.hint: Replay with a new killer — same case file, different truth

reflection_prompt: Which decision in this run shifted your outcome the most? What signal told you it was the right call?
